overview: Peru proclaimed independence in 1821, decades before this map record begins. The republic encompasses coastal, Andean and Amazonian communities whose histories extend far beyond the state. Its story includes railways and libraries, living textile and pottery knowledge, and the difficult work of confronting political violence.

periods.title: Republican institutions and changing connections
periods.summary: Independence and a brief confederation with Bolivia were followed by continuing political and institutional change.

periods.title: Internal armed conflict
periods.summary: The Truth and Reconciliation Commission examined this period of insurgency, state violence and unequal suffering.

periods.title: Memory and continuing cultural life
periods.summary: Investigations of past violence and community traditions form part of the republic’s continuing history.

items.text: Awajún potters in northern Peru use grinding and polishing stones, wooden tools and brushes made with human hair. They collect materials, shape, fire, decorate and finish their vessels. Designs draw on plants, animals, mountains and stars, turning careful observation into useful objects.

Awajún pots serve for cooking, drinking and sharing food as well as ceremonies. Elder women known as Dukúg pass knowledge to other women in their families. Growing the plants used in production is part of the work, so the craft reaches from garden to hearth.

On Taquile in Lake Titicaca, men and women make textiles as an everyday activity. Garments may be knitted or woven on four-stake ground looms. A knitted chullo keeps ears covered; a wide calendar belt depicts agricultural and ritual cycles.

Taquile’s crafts school helps younger people learn textile skills. Makers have also introduced contemporary images while retaining established techniques. Tourism supplies income, but greater demand can change materials and meaning, a handmade tradition has to negotiate a changing market.

The National Library opened in September 1822 with more than eleven thousand volumes, including books from former Jesuit collections and private gifts. San Martín donated about six hundred. The early republic invested in a place where knowledge could be collected and consulted.

After wartime looting in 1881, Ricardo Palma sought donated books through letters to writers abroad. A devastating fire followed in 1943. Jorge Basadre’s rebuilding effort included professional staff training and a National School of Librarians in 1944: recovering a library required people as well as shelves.

The 1821 founding decree described the library as devoted “a la ilustración universal”, “to universal enlightenment.” The National Library reproduces this Spanish phrase from San Martín’s decree of 28 August. It captures an early republican ambition to support independence through learning.

A railway between Lima and Callao opened in 1851, linking the capital and its port. Railway building later reached other regions: the first locomotive entered Cusco in September 1908. Travel and shipping were being reorganized, but connection arrived at different times in different places.

The Lima mint produced eight-real coins under both royal and republican authority in 1821 to 1822. Their different shields make political change visible in objects used for payment. A person examining two coins can see a revolution in the designs without reading a whole proclamation.

Peru participated in the Peru to Bolivian Confederation from 1836 until its dissolution in 1839. That short-lived arrangement belongs between independence and the later republic. National political structures changed even while towns, farms and trading relationships carried on.

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission documented killings, disappearances and other abuses during the 1980 to 2000 conflict, committed by insurgent organizations and state agents. Rural and Indigenous-language communities suffered disproportionately. Its investigation made those unequal experiences central to the national account.

Families of disappeared people organized to seek information and justice, often with women sustaining the effort through years of uncertainty. The commission recognized their persistence. Public memory was built through the work of relatives and communities, not only through official hearings.

ending.text: Peru continues as a republic. Changes of government, the nineteenth-century confederation and the internal armed conflict altered its institutions without ending the country or its diverse peoples. The map’s 1878 start is a coverage date, not the beginning of Peruvian society.
